title_en: Homily in Time of Famine and Drought
author: Basil of Caesarea
occasion: A severe drought and famine have struck the region; Basil interprets the disaster as divine correction for the people's sins, especially greed and neglect of the poor, and calls them to repentance and almsgiving.
argument: Basil opens by invoking the prophet Amos and describing the drought's devastation. He argues that the disaster is God's corrective punishment for the people's sins, above all their failure to share with the poor. He contrasts their shallow repentance with the Ninevites' wholehearted mourning and urges concrete acts of mercy. He warns that hoarding wealth is useless in famine and that God will judge the unmerciful severely. He closes by urging his hearers to imitate Joseph and the early Christians in generosity, and to prepare the soul as a bride for Christ.

outline.move: Basil introduces the homily with Amos, describes the drought's devastation of sky, earth, springs, and crops, and hopes his hearers will respond better than ancient Israel.
He depicts the farmers' grief and quotes Amos to show that the drought is God's corrective punishment for the people's turning away, especially their failure to share.
He criticizes the congregation's half-hearted prayer and contrasts it with the Ninevites' total repentance, which included even the animals.
He continues the Nineveh example, then challenges his hearers to perform concrete acts of mercy and warns that hoarded wealth will be useless in famine.
He urges self-examination, explains that disasters test both rich and poor, and defends God's power and goodness against those who grumble.
He encourages the poor to endure with thanksgiving, citing Elijah, the Israelite young man in the Babylonian pit, and Israel in the wilderness as examples of God's provision.
He urges giving even from scarcity, promising divine repayment, and describes the horrors of starvation to shame those who pass by the hungry.

He recalls cannibalism during Jerusalem's siege, stresses that Christ identifies with the hungry, and urges immediate generosity, citing the example of the three thousand and the first regiment of Christians.
He exhorts his hearers to imitate Joseph's generosity, to resist greed, to prepare the soul as a bride for Christ, and warns of the coming judgment.

cast.name: Amos
cast.who: Old Testament prophet invoked as a model for proclaiming repentance in time of disaster.

cast.name: Elijah
cast.who: Prophet fed by ravens during famine; example of God's provision for the righteous.

cast.name: Job
cast.who: Righteous sufferer whose patient endurance Basil holds up as a model.

cast.name: Joseph
cast.who: Patriarch who fed his family during famine; model of generosity even to enemies.

cast.name: Habakkuk
cast.who: Prophet carried by an angel to feed the Israelite young man in the Babylonian pit.

cast.name: The Israelite young man
cast.who: Young Israelite captive in the Babylonian pit, fed by Habakkuk; traditionally identified with Daniel, but not named in the source.

cast.name: Achan
cast.who: Old Testament figure whose sacrilege brought punishment on all Israel.

cast.name: Zimri
cast.who: Israelite whose immorality with Midianite women brought a plague on Israel.

cast.name: Josephus
cast.who: Jewish historian cited for the famine cannibalism during Jerusalem's siege.

cast.name: Widow of Zarephath
cast.who: Sidonian widow who shared her last food with Elijah and was miraculously provided for.

voices.speaker: Basil (quoting the poor man's prayer)
voices.how_marked: introduced as a model prayer to say

voices.speaker: Widow of Zarephath (quoted)
voices.how_marked: introduced as her words from the story

voices.speaker: The Lord (quoted)
voices.how_marked: introduced with φησίν as a divine saying, not explicitly attributed to Christ in the source

voices.speaker: The Psalmist (quoted)
voices.how_marked: introduced as the Psalmist's general prophecy about the whole body, which Basil then applies to each individual soul

key_terms.sense: famine, the central disaster afflicting the region
drought, the cause of the famine
repentance, the turning back to God Basil demands
love for fellow Christians, shown by sharing goods
greed, the chief sin Basil identifies as causing the disaster
one who shares or gives to others, the righteous person in the last judgment
one who refuses to share, condemned in the last judgment
stored-up wealth, which Basil says is useless in famine
commandment, especially the command to love and give
the final judgment, when the merciful and unmerciful will be separated
thanksgiving to God, which Basil urges even in hardship
almsgiving, concrete aid to the poor
trial or test, the purpose of the disaster for the faithful

names.Pentephres: the Egyptian master to whom Joseph was faithful, traditionally identified with Potiphar

scripture: Basil uses the Septuagint (LXX) and its book names and Psalm numbering. He cites Amos, Job, the Psalms, and the Gospels. Modern citations should follow standard English Bible conventions: e.g., Amos 4:7-8; Job 19:21; Psalm 45:9-11 (LXX Psalm 44); Matthew 25:35-36; Mark 8:2.
uncertain: The exact date of the homily
Whether the addressee is specifically the church at Caesarea or a wider audience
The precise identity of the 'three thousand' early Christians Basil mentions in section 8
Whether the Israelite young man in the Babylonian pit is Daniel
Whether Πεντεφρῇ is the same person as Potiphar

_unresolved_facts.claim: The Israelite young man ... traditionally identified with Daniel, but not named in the source
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Εἶχε δὲ καὶ ὁ Βαβυλώνιος λάκκος τὸν Ἰσραηλίτην νεανίσκον
_unresolved_facts.fix: The Israelite young man in the Babylonian pit, fed by Habakkuk; not named in the source. The biblical story (Bel and the Dragon, LXX Daniel 14:33-39) identifies him as Daniel, but Basil does not name him.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The Lord (quoted) ... not explicitly attributed to Christ in the source
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Σπλαγχνίζομαι γὰρ, φησὶν, ἐπὶ τὸν ὄχλον
_unresolved_facts.fix: The Lord (quoted) ... introduced with φησίν as a divine saying; in context this is Christ's words from the Gospels (cf. Mark 8:2), though Basil does not explicitly name 'Christ' here

_unresolved_facts.claim: Pentephres: the Egyptian master to whom Joseph was faithful, traditionally identified with Potiphar
_unresolved_facts.fix: Pentephres: the Egyptian master to whom Joseph was faithful; the name as given in the LXX (Genesis 37:36, 39:1 etc.), distinct from but often identified with Potiphar

_unresolved_facts.claim: Babylonian pit: lions' den in Babylon
_unresolved_facts.fix: Babylonian pit: the lions' pit/den in Babylon where the Israelite young man was thrown; the story is from Bel and the Dragon (LXX Daniel 14), not the canonical Daniel 6

_unresolved_facts.claim: sections ["8"]: He recalls cannibalism during Jerusalem's siege, stresses that Christ identifies with the hungry
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ὁρᾷς καὶ αὐτὸν τὸν ἡμέτερον Θεὸν τὰ μὲν ἄλλα τῶν παθῶν πολλάκις παρατρέχοντα, ἐπὶ δὲ τοῖς πεινῶσι συμπαθῶς σπλαγχνιζόμενον
_unresolved_facts.fix: He recalls cannibalism during Jerusalem's siege, stresses that God (ὁ ἡμέτερος Θεός) shows special compassion for the hungry
